concepts.def: A coordinate system (an origin and a set of axes) together with synchronized clocks, used by an observer to assign a position (x, y, z) and a time t to every event. Motion is always described relative to a chosen reference frame; the same motion has different descriptions in different frames.

Something that happens at a single point in space at a single instant of time, such as a lamp flashing or a particle decaying. In a given reference frame an event is specified by its coordinates (x, y, z, t); in this topic motion is along x, so (x, t) is enough.

A reference frame that is not accelerating: it is at rest or moving with constant velocity (constant speed in a constant direction) relative to other inertial frames. In an inertial frame Newton's first law holds: a body with no resultant force on it stays at rest or moves with constant velocity. A frame that speeds up, slows down or changes direction (including one moving in a circle at constant speed) is not inertial. The Earth's surface is usually treated as an inertial frame to a good approximation.

The principle that Newton's laws of motion are the same in all inertial reference frames. No experiment in mechanics carried out inside a closed laboratory can tell whether the laboratory is at rest or moving with constant velocity; there is no preferred inertial frame and no absolute state of rest.

The equations x′ = x − vt and t′ = t that give the coordinates (x′, t′) of an event in frame S′ from its coordinates (x, t) in frame S, where S′ moves with constant velocity v along the positive x-direction relative to S and the origins coincide at t = t′ = 0. The equation t′ = t expresses the Galilean assumption that time is absolute: all inertial observers assign the same time to every event, so time intervals and simultaneity are the same in every frame.

The result u′ = u − v, obtained from the Galilean transformation, relating the velocity u of an object measured in S to its velocity u′ measured in S′, where S′ moves at velocity v relative to S along x. Velocities are signed: a velocity in the negative x-direction is negative. Because v is constant, both frames measure the same acceleration. The equation is an excellent approximation at everyday speeds but fails at speeds comparable to c; applied to light it would give c − v, which experiment does not show.

The two assumptions on which special relativity is built: (1) the laws of physics are the same in all inertial reference frames; (2) the speed of light in a vacuum, c, is the same for all inertial observers, whatever the motion of the source or of the observer. The first extends Galilean relativity from mechanics to all of physics, including electromagnetism; the second contradicts Galilean velocity addition.

concepts.term: Speed of light in a vacuum, c
concepts.def: The speed at which light (and all electromagnetic radiation) travels in a vacuum, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ to three significant figures; unit m s⁻¹. By the second postulate it has the same value in every inertial frame. It is the speed of light in a vacuum only; light travels more slowly in a material medium.

γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²), where v is the relative speed of two inertial frames. It has no unit. γ = 1 when v = 0, it is greater than 1 for any non-zero v, and it increases without limit as v approaches c. It depends on v² and so is the same for motion in either direction. For v = 0.60c, γ = 1.25; for v = 0.80c, γ = 1.67 (5/3).

The equations x′ = γ(x − vt) and t′ = γ(t − vx/c²) that give the coordinates of an event in S′ from its coordinates in S, where S′ moves at velocity v along +x relative to S and the origins coincide at t = t′ = 0. They follow from the two postulates. Unlike the Galilean transformation, the time t′ depends on the position x of the event, so time is not absolute. When v ≪ c, γ ≈ 1 and vx/c² ≈ 0, and the equations reduce to the Galilean ones.

u′ = (u − v)/(1 − uv/c²), obtained from the Lorentz transformation, where u is the velocity of an object in S, v is the velocity of S′ relative to S, and u′ is the object's velocity in S′; all velocities are along x and signed. The result never exceeds c in magnitude when |u| and |v| are at most c, and putting u = c gives u′ = c, in agreement with the second postulate. When u, v ≪ c the term uv/c² is negligible and the equation reduces to u′ = u − v.

For two events separated by a time Δt and a distance Δx in some inertial frame, (Δs)² = (cΔt)² − (Δx)². Δs has the unit of length (m). Although Δt and Δx separately differ from frame to frame, every inertial observer calculates the same value of (Δs)²: the interval is invariant. For two events at the same place, Δs = cΔt₀, where Δt₀ is the proper time interval.

A quantity that has the same value in every inertial reference frame. In special relativity the speed of light in a vacuum and the space–time interval are invariant; time intervals, lengths and simultaneity are not. An invariant quantity is different from a conserved quantity: momentum is conserved in a collision but has different values in different frames.

The time interval between two events measured in the inertial frame in which the two events occur at the same place, so that a single clock can be present at both. Unit: s. It is the shortest time interval between the two events measured in any inertial frame, and it is related to the interval by Δt₀ = Δs/c.

The length of an object measured in the inertial frame in which the object is at rest (its rest frame). Unit: m. It is the greatest length of the object measured in any inertial frame; observers moving along its length measure a shorter length.

The time interval Δt between two events measured in an inertial frame in which the events occur at different places is longer than the proper time interval Δt₀ between them: Δt = γΔt₀. Each inertial observer measures clocks moving relative to them to run slow by the factor γ; the effect is reciprocal, and it is a real difference in measured time, not an effect of the travel time of light signals. On S's space–time diagram, a clock at rest at the origin of S′ has the ct′ axis as its world line; its tick at ct′ = 1 (marked with the curve of constant interval) lies on the line ct = γ, so S measures γ units of time for one unit on the moving clock.

The length L of an object measured in an inertial frame in which it moves at speed v is shorter than its proper length L₀: L = L₀/γ. The contraction occurs only along the direction of relative motion; dimensions perpendicular to the motion are unchanged. Like time dilation, it is reciprocal and it is a measured result, not an optical appearance. On S's space–time diagram, the two ends of a rod at rest in S′ have world lines parallel to the ct′ axis; S measures the rod's length between them along a line of constant ct (both ends at the same time in S), and finds L₀/γ.

Two events at different places that are simultaneous in one inertial frame are not simultaneous in a frame moving relative to it along the line joining them. From t′ = γ(t − vx/c²), two events with Δt = 0 and separation Δx in S are separated in S′ by Δt′ = −γvΔx/c²: in S′ the event further along the direction of S′'s motion occurs first. The effect is about when the events happen in each frame, not about when light from them reaches an observer.

A diagram for one inertial frame S with position x on the horizontal axis and ct on the vertical time axis, both in units of length (for example metres or light-years). Each event is a point (x, ct). Because the time axis is ct, a light pulse travels one unit of x for one unit of ct, so its world line is at 45° to both axes. Time dilation, length contraction and the relativity of simultaneity can be read from such diagrams.

The line on a space–time diagram joining all the events in the history of a particle. A particle at rest in S has a world line parallel to the ct axis (vertical); a particle moving at constant velocity has a straight world line tilted from the ct axis by the angle θ where tan θ = v/c; a light pulse has a world line at 45°. In this course world lines are for constant velocity only.

concepts.term: Axes of a moving frame on a space–time diagram
concepts.def: For a frame S′ moving at v along +x relative to S, drawn on S's diagram: the ct′ axis is the world line of the origin of S′ (all events with x′ = 0), tilted from the ct axis by θ with tan θ = v/c; the x′ axis is the set of events with ct′ = 0, tilted by the same angle θ above the x axis. The two primed axes close up symmetrically towards the 45° light line. Any line parallel to the x′ axis joins events that are simultaneous in S′; any line parallel to the ct′ axis joins events at the same place in S′.

concepts.term: Scales on the axes of two frames
concepts.def: The scales on the ct′ and x′ axes are not the same as those on the ct and x axes. They are fixed by lines of constant space–time interval: for example the curve (ct)² − x² = 1 unit² crosses the ct axis at ct = 1 and the ct′ axis at ct′ = 1. On S's diagram that point on the ct′ axis lies further from the origin than ct = 1 does on the ct axis, so one unit on a primed axis is drawn longer.

The angle θ between the world line of a particle moving at constant speed v and the ct axis of a space–time diagram satisfies tan θ = v/c. θ = 0 for a particle at rest, θ = 45° for light, and θ < 45° for every particle with mass, because such a particle's speed is always less than c.

An unstable fundamental particle, similar to an electron but about 207 times more massive, produced in the upper atmosphere (typically 10–15 km up) when cosmic rays collide with atmospheric nuclei. At rest a muon decays with a half-life of about 1.5 μs (mean lifetime about 2.2 μs). Atmospheric muons reach the ground with speeds very close to c.

Experiments that count atmospheric muons of known speed at two different altitudes. The fraction surviving the descent is far greater than the fraction predicted from the rest-frame half-life and the Earth-frame travel time. The result agrees with special relativity when described in either frame: in the Earth frame the muons' half-life is dilated by γ (time dilation); in the muons' frame the distance through the atmosphere is contracted by γ (length contraction). Both descriptions predict the same survival fraction.

mcqs.q: Treat the Earth's surface as an inertial reference frame. Which of the following is also an inertial reference frame?
options: A car going round a circular roundabout at a steady 30 m s⁻¹
A lift at the instant it is at rest while reversing direction
A rocket whose engine gives it a uniform acceleration of 3 m s⁻²
A train on a straight, level track at a steady 30 m s⁻¹
mcqs.specStatementText: reference frames
mcqs.explain: The train's velocity (speed and direction) is constant, so it is not accelerating. A non-accelerating frame is an inertial frame: in it a ball placed on a table stays at rest, just as it would on the ground.
mcqs.working: Inertial frame = non-accelerating. Train: straight track, constant speed → constant velocity, a = 0. Roundabout: direction changes, a = v²/r ≠ 0. Reversing lift: v = 0 momentarily but Δv/Δt ≠ 0. Rocket: a = 3 m s⁻² ≠ 0.
rationales: A student who equates constant speed with constant velocity picks this. The car's direction is changing, so it has a centripetal acceleration and its frame is not inertial.
A student who thinks zero velocity means zero acceleration picks this. The lift's velocity is changing through zero, so it is accelerating at that instant and its frame is not inertial.
A student who reads 'uniform' as 'steady motion' picks this. A uniform acceleration is still an acceleration, and an inertial frame must be non-accelerating.

The train's velocity (speed and direction) is constant, so it is not accelerating. A non-accelerating frame is an inertial frame: in it a ball placed on a table stays at rest, just as it would on the ground.

mcqs.q: A passenger on a train moving at constant velocity says that the platform is moving backwards at 20 m s⁻¹. A person standing on the platform says that the train is moving forwards at 20 m s⁻¹. Which statement is correct?
options: Only the platform observer is correct, because the ground is the frame truly at rest.
Both are correct: each describes the motion relative to their own inertial frame.
Only the platform observer is correct, as a moving frame cannot be inertial.
Only one can be correct, as velocity belongs to the object, not to the observer.
mcqs.specStatementText: reference frames
mcqs.explain: Motion is always described relative to a reference frame. The train and the platform are both inertial frames, and neither is preferred, so both descriptions are equally valid.
mcqs.working: Train frame: platform velocity −20 m s⁻¹. Platform frame: train velocity +20 m s⁻¹. Both frames are inertial (constant velocity), so both descriptions are valid.
rationales: A student who believes the ground is the one frame that is really at rest picks this. The ground itself moves relative to the Sun; no inertial frame is preferred.
Motion is always described relative to a reference frame. The train and the platform are both inertial frames, and neither is preferred, so both descriptions are equally valid.
A student who thinks an inertial frame must be at rest picks this. A frame moving at constant velocity is inertial, so the passenger's frame is as valid as the platform's.

A student who thinks each object has a single true velocity picks this. Velocity is always measured relative to a frame, so the platform has one velocity in the train's frame and the train another in the platform's frame, and both are valid.

mcqs.q: A passenger in a train moving along a straight track at constant velocity drops a ball from rest relative to the train. Where does the ball land, and why?
options: Behind the point of release, as the floor moves on while the ball is falling.
Directly below the point of release, as the air in the carriage carries it.
Directly below the point of release, as it keeps the train's horizontal velocity.
Directly below the point of release, and it falls vertically for the platform.
mcqs.specStatementText: that Newton's laws of motion are the same in all inertial reference frames and this is known as Galilean relativity
mcqs.explain: Before release the ball moves with the train. No horizontal force acts after release, so it keeps that horizontal velocity and stays level with the release point. Galilean relativity: the result is the same as in a stationary train.
mcqs.working: Train frame: horizontal velocity 0, falls vertically, lands below release point. Platform frame: horizontal velocity = train's velocity, parabolic path; lands at the point that is then below the release point.
rationales: A student who thinks a released object is 'left behind' picks this. The ball already has the train's horizontal velocity and nothing changes it, so it keeps pace with the floor.

A student who credits the moving air with keeping objects up with the train picks this. The ball keeps the train's velocity by Newton's first law. The carriage air moves with the train and exerts no horizontal push; the result is the same in a vacuum.

Before release the ball moves with the train. No horizontal force acts after release, so it keeps that horizontal velocity and stays level with the release point. Galilean relativity: the result is the same as in a stationary train.

A student who thinks the ball's motion is the same in every frame picks this. On the platform the ball has the train's horizontal velocity as it falls, so it follows a curved (parabolic) path, not a vertical line.

mcqs.q: Observers in two inertial frames, S and S′, which move at a constant velocity relative to each other, both study a puck that is being pushed across ice and is accelerating. Which quantity do they measure to have the same value?
options: The acceleration of the puck at any instant
The velocity of the puck at any given instant
The linear momentum of the puck at any instant
The position of the puck at any instant
mcqs.specStatementText: that Newton's laws of motion are the same in all inertial reference frames and this is known as Galilean relativity
mcqs.explain: u′ = u − v with v constant, so Δu′ = Δu and the accelerations are equal. Both observers therefore find the same resultant force, F = ma: Newton's laws are the same in both frames.
mcqs.working: Galilean: u′ = u − v, v constant → a′ = Δu′/Δt = Δu/Δt = a. Velocity, momentum and position differ between the frames.
rationales: u′ = u − v with v constant, so Δu′ = Δu and the accelerations are equal. Both observers therefore find the same resultant force, F = ma: Newton's laws are the same in both frames.
A student who thinks an object has one velocity for all observers picks this. The velocities differ by the relative velocity of the frames, u′ = u − v.
A student who confuses 'conserved' with 'the same in every frame' picks this. Momentum mu depends on the velocity, which differs between the frames.
A student who thinks positions are the same in every frame picks this. Positions are measured from each frame's own origin, and the origins move apart: x′ = x − vt.

mcqs.q: A ball rolls along a platform at 5.0 m s⁻¹. Frame S is the platform; frame S′ is a train moving at 25 m s⁻¹ in the positive x-direction relative to the platform. The origins of S and S′ coincide at t = 0. At t = 12 s the ball is at x = 450 m in S. What is the ball's position x′ in S′ at that instant?
mcqs.specStatementText: that in Galilean relativity the position x′ and time t′ of an event are given by x′ = x − vt and t′ = t
mcqs.explain: x′ = x − vt, where v is the velocity of S′ relative to S: x′ = 450 m − (25 m s⁻¹)(12 s) = 450 m − 300 m = 150 m.
mcqs.working: x′ = x − vt = 450 m − (25 m s⁻¹ × 12 s) = 450 m − 300 m = 150 m. (The ball's own speed of 5.0 m s⁻¹ is not needed.)
rationales: A student who adds vt, thinking positions in a forward-moving frame are larger, calculates 450 + 300 = 750 m. The origin of S′ has moved 300 m towards the ball, so vt is subtracted.
A student who uses the ball's speed in the transformation calculates 450 − 5.0 × 12 = 390 m. The v in x′ = x − vt is the velocity of frame S′ relative to S, 25 m s⁻¹.
A student who thinks an event has the same position in every frame gives 450 m. The origin of S′ is 300 m from the origin of S at t = 12 s, so the positions differ.
x′ = x − vt, where v is the velocity of S′ relative to S: x′ = 450 m − (25 m s⁻¹)(12 s) = 450 m − 300 m = 150 m.

mcqs.q: In Galilean relativity the time of an event in frame S′ is related to its time in frame S by t′ = t. What does this equation state?
options: Both observers give each event the same time, whatever their relative motion.
Each observer gives a later time to an event the further away from them it happens.
The moving observer's clock runs slow, so it gives a smaller time to each event.
Only the observer at rest gives the true time; the moving one must correct it.
mcqs.specStatementText: that in Galilean relativity the position x′ and time t′ of an event are given by x′ = x − vt and t′ = t
mcqs.explain: t′ = t is the Galilean assumption that time is absolute: all inertial observers assign the same time to every event, so they agree on time intervals and on simultaneity.
mcqs.working: t′ = t for all events → identical time coordinates, intervals and simultaneity in every inertial frame (absolute time).
rationales: t′ = t is the Galilean assumption that time is absolute: all inertial observers assign the same time to every event, so they agree on time intervals and on simultaneity.
A student who dates an event by when its light arrives picks this. The time of an event is read on a clock at the event; t′ = t says the two frames' clocks agree for every event, wherever it is.
A student who carries time dilation into Galilean relativity picks this. Galilean relativity has no time dilation: t′ = t exactly. Slow-running clocks belong to special relativity.
A student who thinks one frame is really at rest picks this. t′ = t says both observers give the same time, so there is nothing to correct and neither frame is preferred.

mcqs.q: On a straight road, car A travels east at 35 m s⁻¹ and car B travels west at 22 m s⁻¹, both relative to the road. Take east as the positive direction. What is the velocity of car B in the reference frame of car A?
options: +57 m s⁻¹
−57 m s⁻¹
−13 m s⁻¹
−22 m s⁻¹
mcqs.specStatementText: that Galilean transformation equations lead to the velocity addition equation as given by u′ = u − v
mcqs.explain: In A's frame, v = +35 m s⁻¹ and B's velocity in the road frame is u = −22 m s⁻¹. u′ = u − v = −22 − 35 = −57 m s⁻¹: B approaches A at 57 m s⁻¹, moving west.
mcqs.working: u = −22 m s⁻¹ (B, road frame), v = +35 m s⁻¹ (A relative to road). u′ = u − v = −22 − 35 = −57 m s⁻¹.
rationales: A student who calculates v − u = 35 − (−22) = +57 m s⁻¹ has found the velocity of A in B's frame. The velocity of B relative to A is u − v, which is negative.
In A's frame, v = +35 m s⁻¹ and B's velocity in the road frame is u = −22 m s⁻¹. u′ = u − v = −22 − 35 = −57 m s⁻¹: B approaches A at 57 m s⁻¹, moving west.
A student who ignores directions and subtracts the speeds gets 22 − 35 = −13 m s⁻¹. B moves west, so u = −22 m s⁻¹, and the magnitudes combine.
A student who thinks B's velocity is the same for every observer gives its road-frame value. In A's frame the relative velocity of the frames must be subtracted: u′ = u − v.

mcqs.q: A spacecraft moves directly away from a laser at 0.50c relative to the laser. Applying u′ = u − v, an observer on the spacecraft should measure the laser light passing at 0.50c. Experiments of this kind find c for every inertial observer. What should be concluded?
options: The experiments must contain an error, since u′ = u − v is common sense.
Light is an exception as it is massless; u′ = u − v holds for massive bodies.
u′ = u − v is only an approximation, valid when speeds are much less than c.
The ship only appears to measure c; relative to it the light really passes at 0.50c.
mcqs.specStatementText: that Galilean transformation equations lead to the velocity addition equation as given by u′ = u − v
mcqs.explain: The Galilean result follows from the assumption t′ = t. It matches experiment at everyday speeds but fails for light and for any object moving at a speed comparable to c. It is replaced by the relativistic u′ = (u − v)/(1 − uv/c²).
mcqs.working: Galilean prediction in spacecraft frame: u′ = c − 0.50c = 0.50c. Measured: c. The Galilean equation is therefore only an approximation; special relativity replaces it.
rationales: A student who treats Galilean addition as exact common sense at all speeds blames the measurement. Many independent experiments, with different methods, all find c for every inertial observer; the equation, not the measurement, is at fault.

A student who thinks light is an exception because it is massless picks this. The Galilean rule also fails for fast electrons and muons; the flaw is the assumption t′ = t, which applies to everything.

The Galilean result follows from the assumption t′ = t. It matches experiment at everyday speeds but fails for light and for any object moving at a speed comparable to c. It is replaced by the relativistic u′ = (u − v)/(1 − uv/c²).

A student who thinks the laser's frame gives the "true" speed, so the ship's measurement is only apparent, picks this. The ship's frame is as valid as any other, and the ship's observer really does measure c; the Galilean prediction of 0.50c is simply wrong.

mcqs.q: Which statement is one of the two postulates of special relativity?
options: No object with mass can reach or exceed the speed of light in a vacuum.
The speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all inertial observers.
Light travels at the same speed in every medium it passes through.
The laws of physics are the same only in frames that are at rest.
mcqs.specStatementText: the two postulates of special relativity
mcqs.explain: This is Einstein's second postulate: c is independent of the motion of source and observer, which contradicts Galilean velocity addition. The first postulate is that the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames.
mcqs.working: Postulate 1: the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames. Postulate 2: the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all inertial observers.
rationales: A student who thinks the speed limit is a starting assumption picks this. That no massive object can reach c is a consequence of the postulates, not one of them.

This is Einstein's second postulate: c is independent of the motion of source and observer, which contradicts Galilean velocity addition. The first postulate is that the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames.
A student who has dropped 'in a vacuum' from the second postulate picks this. Light travels more slowly in glass or water than in a vacuum; the postulate concerns c in a vacuum.

A student who thinks an inertial frame must be at rest picks this. The first postulate applies to every inertial frame, including frames moving at constant velocity; rest is just the special case of zero velocity.

mcqs.q: A spacecraft travels directly towards a distant star at 0.60c relative to the star. An astronaut measures the speed of the starlight arriving at the spacecraft. What does the astronaut find?
options: 1.6c, as the speed of the spacecraft towards the star adds to the speed of light
c, but only as the star is at rest; light from a moving star would be faster
0.40c, as the spacecraft's speed is subtracted from the speed of light
c, as the speed of light in a vacuum does not depend on the motion of the observer
mcqs.specStatementText: the two postulates of special relativity
mcqs.explain: By the second postulate every inertial observer measures the speed of light in a vacuum to be c, whatever the motion of source or observer. The spacecraft's speed changes the light's frequency and wavelength, not its speed.
mcqs.working: Second postulate: the speed of light in a vacuum = c for all inertial observers. Neither Galilean addition (c + 0.60c = 1.6c) nor subtraction of speeds (c − 0.60c = 0.40c) applies; the astronaut measures c.
rationales: A student who applies Galilean velocity addition to light adds the speeds. Experiment shows light has speed c for all inertial observers, so u′ = u − v does not apply to light.
A student who thinks a moving source changes the speed of light picks this. The second postulate states that c is independent of the motion of the source as well as of the observer.

A student who finds a relative speed by subtracting the smaller speed from the larger, ignoring that the spacecraft and the light are moving towards each other, gets c − 0.60c = 0.40c. By the second postulate the speed of light in a vacuum is c for all inertial observers, so the astronaut measures c.

By the second postulate every inertial observer measures the speed of light in a vacuum to be c, whatever the motion of source or observer. The spacecraft's speed changes the light's frequency and wavelength, not its speed.

mcqs.q: Frame S′ moves at v = 0.80c in the positive x-direction relative to frame S, and the origins coincide at t = t′ = 0. An event occurs at x = 900 m, t = 1.0 μs in S. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. What is the position x′ of the event in S′?
mcqs.specStatementText: that the postulates of special relativity lead to the Lorentz transformation equations for the coordinates of an event in two inertial reference frames as given by x′ = γ(x − vt); t′ = γ(t − vx/c²) where γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²)
rationales: A student who leaves out γ calculates x − vt = 900 − 240 = 660 m, which is the Galilean value. At 0.80c, γ = 1.67 multiplies the bracket.
A student who divides by γ calculates 660/1.67 = 396 m. The Lorentz transformation multiplies (x − vt) by γ.
A student who adds vt calculates 1.67 × (900 + 240) = 1900 m. The origin of S′ has moved 240 m towards the event, so vt is subtracted.

mcqs.q: Frame S′ moves at v = 0.80c in the positive x-direction relative to frame S, and the origins coincide at t = t′ = 0. An event occurs at x = 900 m, t = 1.0 μs in S. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. What is the time t′ of the event in S′?
mcqs.specStatementText: that the postulates of special relativity lead to the Lorentz transformation equations for the coordinates of an event in two inertial reference frames as given by x′ = γ(x − vt); t′ = γ(t − vx/c²) where γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²)
mcqs.explain: γ = 1.67. vx/c² = (0.80 × 3.00 × 10⁸ × 900)/(3.00 × 10⁸)² = 2.4 × 10⁻⁶ s. t′ = γ(t − vx/c²) = 1.67 × (1.0 − 2.4) μs = 1.67 × (−1.4 μs) = −2.3 μs. The event happens before the origins pass, according to S′.
rationales: γ = 1.67. vx/c² = (0.80 × 3.00 × 10⁸ × 900)/(3.00 × 10⁸)² = 2.4 × 10⁻⁶ s. t′ = γ(t − vx/c²) = 1.67 × (1.0 − 2.4) μs = 1.67 × (−1.4 μs) = −2.3 μs. The event happens before the origins pass, according to S′.
A student who assumes time is the same in every frame (t′ = t) gives 1.0 μs. In special relativity t′ depends on the position of the event through the vx/c² term.
A student who leaves out γ calculates t − vx/c² = −1.4 μs. The bracket must be multiplied by γ = 1.67.
A student who applies time dilation to the event's time coordinate calculates γt = 1.67 × 1.0 = 1.7 μs. The full transformation t′ = γ(t − vx/c²) includes the position-dependent term.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the Lorentz factor γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²) is correct?
options: It is never greater than 1, and it decreases towards zero as v approaches c.
It increases in direct proportion to v, so it equals 2 when v is half of c.
It is larger for a frame approaching the observer than for one moving away at the same speed.
It is never less than 1, and it increases without limit as v approaches c.
mcqs.specStatementText: that the postulates of special relativity lead to the Lorentz transformation equations for the coordinates of an event in two inertial reference frames as given by x′ = γ(x − vt); t′ = γ(t − vx/c²) where γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²)
mcqs.explain: γ = 1 at v = 0, is greater than 1 for any non-zero v, and 1 − v²/c² tends to zero as v approaches c, so γ grows without limit. It has the same value for either direction of motion.
mcqs.working: γ(0) = 1; γ(0.50c) = 1/√0.75 = 1.15; γ(0.87c) ≈ 2.0; γ → ∞ as v → c. Depends on v², so direction does not matter.
rationales: A student who takes γ to be √(1 − v²/c²) itself, rather than its reciprocal, picks this. √(1 − v²/c²) is at most 1, so its reciprocal γ is at least 1.
A student who assumes a linear relationship picks this. At 0.50c, γ = 1/√0.75 = 1.15; γ reaches 2 only at v = 0.87c.
A student who expects γ to behave like the Doppler shift picks this. γ depends on v², so approach and recession at the same speed give the same γ.
γ = 1 at v = 0, is greater than 1 for any non-zero v, and 1 − v²/c² tends to zero as v approaches c, so γ grows without limit. It has the same value for either direction of motion.

mcqs.q: In the Earth's frame S, spacecraft A moves at +0.60c and spacecraft B moves at −0.50c along the same line, towards each other. Frame S′ is the rest frame of A. Using u′ = (u − v)/(1 − uv/c²), what is the velocity of B in S′?
mcqs.specStatementText: that Lorentz transformation equations lead to the relativistic velocity addition equation as given by u′ = (u − v)/(1 − uv/c²)
rationales: A student who uses Galilean addition, u − v = −0.50c − 0.60c, gets −1.10c. That exceeds c; the relativistic denominator 1 − uv/c² = 1.30 is needed.
A student who drops the signs in the denominator uses 1 − 0.30 = 0.70 and gets −1.10c/0.70 = −1.57c. uv = (−0.50c)(0.60c) is negative, so the denominator is 1 + 0.30 = 1.30.
A student who treats B's velocity as +0.50c (ignoring its direction) gets (0.50 − 0.60)/(1 − 0.30) = −0.14c. B moves in the negative direction, so u = −0.50c.

mcqs.q: An aircraft flies at 250 m s⁻¹ relative to the ground and a faster jet flies in the same direction at 800 m s⁻¹. A student compares u′ = u − v = 550 m s⁻¹ for the jet in the aircraft's frame with the relativistic value from u′ = (u − v)/(1 − uv/c²). Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Which evaluation is correct?
options: The relativistic equation cannot be used, as relativity applies only to speeds near c.
u − v is exact at these speeds, so the relativistic equation gives a slightly wrong value.
uv/c² ≈ 2 × 10⁻¹², so the Galilean value differs from the relativistic one by a negligible amount.
uv/c² ≈ 7 × 10⁻⁴, so the Galilean value is in error by about 0.07 %, which is a clearly measurable amount.
mcqs.specStatementText: that Lorentz transformation equations lead to the relativistic velocity addition equation as given by u′ = (u − v)/(1 − uv/c²)
mcqs.explain: uv/c² = (800 × 250)/(3.00 × 10⁸)² = 2.2 × 10⁻¹². The relativistic value differs from 550 m s⁻¹ by about 1 × 10⁻⁹ m s⁻¹, so u′ = u − v is an excellent approximation at everyday speeds.
rationales: A student who thinks relativity switches on only near c picks this. The relativistic equation is valid at every speed; at 800 m s⁻¹ it simply gives a result extremely close to the Galilean one.
A student who treats Galilean addition as exact picks this. The relativistic equation is the exact one; the Galilean result is the approximation, though the difference is negligible here.
uv/c² = (800 × 250)/(3.00 × 10⁸)² = 2.2 × 10⁻¹². The relativistic value differs from 550 m s⁻¹ by about 1 × 10⁻⁹ m s⁻¹, so u′ = u − v is an excellent approximation at everyday speeds.
A student who divides by c instead of c² gets 800 × 250/(3.00 × 10⁸) = 6.7 × 10⁻⁴. That quantity has a unit (m s⁻¹) and cannot be subtracted from 1; with c² the term is 2.2 × 10⁻¹².

mcqs.q: Two inertial observers in relative motion measure the same two events. Which quantity do they necessarily agree on?
options: The time interval Δt between the events, as time passes at an equal rate for every observer
The quantity (cΔt)² − (Δx)², the square of the space–time interval between the events
The distance Δx between the two events, as distances do not depend on the frame
The quantity (cΔt)² + (Δx)², the square of the straight-line distance on a space–time diagram
mcqs.specStatementText: that the space–time interval Δs between two events is an invariant quantity as given by (Δs)² = (cΔt)² − (Δx)²
mcqs.explain: The space–time interval is invariant: every inertial observer calculates the same (Δs)² = (cΔt)² − (Δx)², even though they measure different Δt and Δx.
mcqs.working: Invariant: (Δs)² = (cΔt)² − (Δx)². Δt and Δx individually depend on the frame.
rationales: A student who assumes absolute time picks this. In special relativity Δt depends on the frame (for example time dilation); only the combination (cΔt)² − (Δx)² is invariant.
The space–time interval is invariant: every inertial observer calculates the same (Δs)² = (cΔt)² − (Δx)², even though they measure different Δt and Δx.
A student who thinks distances are the same in every frame picks this. Δx differs between frames even in Galilean relativity when the events are not simultaneous.
A student who applies Pythagoras' theorem to space–time picks this. The invariant has a minus sign: (Δs)² = (cΔt)² − (Δx)².

mcqs.q: In frame S, two events occur at the same place, 5.0 μs apart. In frame S′, which moves relative to S, the two events are 1200 m apart. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. What is the time interval between the events in S′?
options: 3.0 μs
9.0 μs
5.0 μs
6.4 μs
mcqs.specStatementText: that the space–time interval Δs between two events is an invariant quantity as given by (Δs)² = (cΔt)² − (Δx)²
rationales: A student who takes (Δs)² = (cΔt)² + (Δx)² writes 1500² = (cΔt′)² + 1200² and gets cΔt′ = 900 m, Δt′ = 3.0 μs. With the correct minus sign, (cΔt′)² = 1500² + 1200².
A student who uses Δs = cΔt − Δx without squares writes 1500 = cΔt′ − 1200, giving cΔt′ = 2700 m and 9.0 μs. Only the squared combination is invariant.
A student who assumes time intervals are the same in every frame gives 5.0 μs. Δt changes between frames; it is (Δs)² that is invariant.

mcqs.q: A muon is created in the upper atmosphere and later decays, moving at 0.99c relative to the Earth throughout. Which observer measures the proper time interval between its creation and its decay?
options: An observer moving with the muon, as both events occur at the same place in that frame
An observer at rest on the Earth, as the Earth is the frame that is not moving
Any observer with an accurate clock, as proper time means the correct time
An observer midway between the events, as light from each reaches them equally fast
mcqs.specStatementText: proper time interval and proper length
mcqs.explain: The proper time interval is measured in the frame in which the two events occur at the same place. In the muon's rest frame it is created and decays at the same point, so a single clock there measures Δt₀.
mcqs.working: Proper time: frame in which both events occur at the same place → muon rest frame.
rationales: The proper time interval is measured in the frame in which the two events occur at the same place. In the muon's rest frame it is created and decays at the same point, so a single clock there measures Δt₀.
A student who treats the Earth as truly at rest picks this. In the Earth frame the creation and decay happen kilometres apart, so the Earth measures a dilated interval, not the proper time.
A student who reads 'proper' as 'correct' picks this. Every inertial observer's measurement is correct for their frame; the proper time is the one measured where both events happen at the same place.

A student who thinks event times depend on when light arrives picks this. Signal delay is always corrected for; the proper time is defined by the two events being at the same place, not by the observer's position.

mcqs.q: An astronaut measures the length of her spacecraft. An observer on Earth, relative to whom the spacecraft moves at 0.60c along its length, also measures it. Which statement is correct?
options: The astronaut measures the proper length, the shortest length found by any inertial observer.
The Earth observer measures the proper length, as the Earth is the frame that is truly at rest.
The astronaut measures the proper length, the longest length found by any inertial observer.
Both measure the same length; the Earth observer merely sees it shorter because light takes time.
mcqs.specStatementText: proper time interval and proper length
mcqs.explain: The proper length is measured in the object's rest frame, the astronaut's. Every observer moving along its length measures L = L₀/γ, which is shorter.
mcqs.working: Proper length L₀: measured in the rest frame of the object (astronaut). Earth: L = L₀/γ = L₀/1.25 = 0.80L₀.
rationales: A student who reasons that proper length must be the shortest, like proper time, picks this. Proper time is the shortest interval but proper length is the longest length: L = L₀/γ ≤ L₀.
A student who treats the Earth as truly at rest picks this. The proper length is measured in the frame in which the object is at rest, which here is the astronaut's frame.
The proper length is measured in the object's rest frame, the astronaut's. Every observer moving along its length measures L = L₀/γ, which is shorter.
A student who thinks length contraction is an optical effect picks this. After allowing for light travel time the Earth observer still measures L = L₀/γ, a real difference.

mcqs.q: A spacecraft passes the Earth at 0.80c. A lamp on the spacecraft flashes once every 6.00 min, measured by a clock on the spacecraft. Earth observers time the flashes using clocks at rest in the Earth's frame. What time interval between flashes do they measure?
options: 3.60 min
10.0 min
16.7 min
13.4 min
mcqs.specStatementText: time dilation as given by Δt = γΔt₀
mcqs.explain: The spacecraft's clock is present at every flash, so 6.00 min is the proper time Δt₀. γ = 1/√(1 − 0.80²) = 1.667, so Δt = γΔt₀ = 1.667 × 6.00 = 10.0 min.
mcqs.working: Δt₀ = 6.00 min (spacecraft clock at both flashes). γ = 1/√(1 − 0.80²) = 1/√0.36 = 1.667. Δt = γΔt₀ = 1.667 × 6.00 min = 10.0 min.
rationales: A student who thinks the Earth measures the shorter interval divides by γ: 6.00/1.667 = 3.60 min. The proper time, measured on the spacecraft, is the shortest interval; the Earth measures γΔt₀.
The spacecraft's clock is present at every flash, so 6.00 min is the proper time Δt₀. γ = 1/√(1 − 0.80²) = 1.667, so Δt = γΔt₀ = 1.667 × 6.00 = 10.0 min.
A student who omits the square root uses γ = 1/(1 − 0.64) = 2.78, giving 16.7 min. γ = 1/√0.36 = 1.667.
A student who does not square v/c uses γ = 1/√(1 − 0.80) = 2.24, giving 13.4 min. v²/c² = 0.64, so γ = 1.667.

mcqs.q: Spacecraft A and B pass each other at a relative speed of 0.60c. Each carries an identical clock. The astronaut in A says that B's clock runs slow, and the astronaut in B says that A's clock runs slow. Which evaluation is correct?
options: Only one can be correct: the clock that is really moving is the one that runs slow.
Neither is correct: the clocks only appear slow because light from them takes time to arrive.
Both are correct: each measures the clock moving relative to them to run slow, by γ = 1.25.
Neither is correct: the two effects cancel, so each measures the other's clock at the normal rate.
mcqs.specStatementText: time dilation as given by Δt = γΔt₀
mcqs.explain: By the first postulate neither inertial frame is preferred, so time dilation is reciprocal. Each observer measures the other's clock to run slow by γ = 1/√(1 − 0.60²) = 1.25. The relativity of simultaneity makes the two results consistent.
mcqs.working: γ = 1/√(1 − 0.60²) = 1/0.80 = 1.25. Each frame measures the other's clock interval as Δt = 1.25Δt₀.
rationales: A student who believes one spacecraft is 'really' moving picks this. There is no absolute rest; each astronaut can regard their own craft as at rest, and both measurements are valid.
A student who treats time dilation as a signal-delay illusion picks this. Each observer's result remains after correcting for light travel time; it is a real measured effect.

By the first postulate neither inertial frame is preferred, so time dilation is reciprocal. Each observer measures the other's clock to run slow by γ = 1/√(1 − 0.60²) = 1.25. The relativity of simultaneity makes the two results consistent.
A student who sees reciprocal time dilation as a contradiction picks this. The two measurements compare different pairs of events in different frames, so they do not cancel; each is valid.

mcqs.q: A spacecraft has a proper length of 60.0 m. It moves past a space station at 0.60c along its length. What length does an observer on the space station measure for the spacecraft?
mcqs.specStatementText: length contraction as given by L = L₀/γ
mcqs.explain: γ = 1/√(1 − 0.60²) = 1.25. L = L₀/γ = 60 m/1.25 = 48 m. The spacecraft is shorter along its direction of motion.
rationales: A student who multiplies by γ, as in time dilation, gets 60.0 × 1.25 = 75 m. A moving object is measured shorter: L = L₀/γ.
A student who omits the square root in γ uses 1/(1 − 0.36) = 1.5625 and gets 38 m. γ = 1/√0.64 = 1.25.
A student who thinks contraction is only an optical appearance gives the proper length. The station observer really measures L = L₀/γ = 48 m.
γ = 1/√(1 − 0.60²) = 1.25. L = L₀/γ = 60 m/1.25 = 48 m. The spacecraft is shorter along its direction of motion.

mcqs.q: A lamp at the exact centre of a railway carriage flashes once. The carriage moves at constant high speed past a platform. In the carriage frame, the light reaches the front and rear doors at the same time. According to an observer on the platform, what happens?
options: The light reaches the rear door first, as the rear door moves towards the light.
Both at once, as light going forwards moves at c + v and backwards at c − v.
Both at once, as events simultaneous in one frame are simultaneous in every frame.
The light arrives at both doors together; she only sees one first because it is nearer to her.
mcqs.specStatementText: the relativity of simultaneity
mcqs.explain: In the platform frame both pulses travel at c (second postulate). The rear door moves towards its pulse and the front door away from its pulse, so the rear door is reached first. Events simultaneous in the carriage frame are not simultaneous in the platform frame.
mcqs.working: Platform frame: both pulses at c; rear door approaches its pulse, front door recedes from its pulse → rear door reached first.
rationales: In the platform frame both pulses travel at c (second postulate). The rear door moves towards its pulse and the front door away from its pulse, so the rear door is reached first. Events simultaneous in the carriage frame are not simultaneous in the platform frame.
A student who applies Galilean velocity addition to light picks this. In the platform frame both pulses travel at c, so the rear door, moving towards its pulse, is reached first.

A student who assumes absolute simultaneity picks this. Simultaneity is relative: events at different places that are simultaneous in one frame are not simultaneous in a frame moving along the line joining them.
A student who thinks the disagreement is a light-delay effect picks this. Even after correcting for light travel time to the observer, the platform frame assigns the rear-door event the earlier time.

mcqs.q: Two events are simultaneous in frame S and are 1200 m apart along the x-axis. Frame S′ moves at 0.60c along the x-axis relative to S. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. What is the magnitude of the time interval between the events in S′?
options: 2.4 μs
3.0 μs
1.9 μs
4.0 μs
mcqs.specStatementText: the relativity of simultaneity
rationales: A student who leaves out γ gives vΔx/c² = 2.4 μs. The Lorentz transformation multiplies the bracket by γ = 1.25.
A student who divides by γ gets 2.4/1.25 = 1.9 μs. In t′ = γ(t − vx/c²) the bracket is multiplied by γ.

A student who thinks the time difference is the light travel time between the events calculates Δx/c = 1200/(3.00 × 10⁸) = 4.0 μs. The relativity of simultaneity comes from the vx/c² term, not from signal delay.

mcqs.q: A space–time diagram for frame S has x on the horizontal axis and ct on the vertical axis, with equal scales. Which describes the world lines of a particle at rest in S and of a light pulse?
options: Particle: a single point on the x axis of the diagram. Light pulse: a line at 45° to both axes.
Particle: a line parallel to the x axis. Light pulse: a line at 45° to both axes.
Particle: a line parallel to the ct axis. Light pulse: a line at 45° to both axes.
Particle: a line parallel to the ct axis. Light pulse: a line along the x axis.
mcqs.specStatementText: space–time diagrams
mcqs.explain: A particle at rest keeps the same x as ct increases, so its world line is vertical. Light travels a distance cΔt in time Δt, so Δx = Δ(ct) and its world line is at 45°.
mcqs.working: At rest: x constant → line parallel to ct axis. Light: Δx = cΔt = Δ(ct) → 45°.
rationales: A student who reads the diagram as a picture of the path in space picks this. The particle exists at every instant, so it has an event at every ct: a vertical line, not a point.
A student who reads the diagram like a distance–time graph picks this. Here time (ct) is vertical, so a horizontal line joins events at one instant; a particle at rest has a vertical world line.
A particle at rest keeps the same x as ct increases, so its world line is vertical. Light travels a distance cΔt in time Δt, so Δx = Δ(ct) and its world line is at 45°.
A student who treats light as instantaneous picks this. With ct on the time axis, light moves one unit of x for each unit of ct, so its world line is at 45°, not horizontal.

mcqs.q: A space–time diagram for frame S (axes x and ct) also shows the axes x′ and ct′ of a frame S′ moving relative to S. How are the scales on the ct′ and x′ axes determined?
options: They are set by lines of constant space–time interval, so their units differ from those on ct and x.
They are identical to the scales on ct and x, because all four axes are measured in metres.
They are shrunk by γ, because moving clocks run slow and moving lengths are contracted.
They are stretched by γ on ct′ and shrunk by γ on x′, by time dilation and length contraction.
mcqs.specStatementText: space–time diagrams
mcqs.explain: The guide states that the scales are not the same and are defined by lines of constant space–time interval. The curve (ct)² − x² = 1 unit² crosses ct′ at ct′ = 1; on S's diagram that point lies further from the origin than ct = 1.
mcqs.working: Scale on ct′: where (ct)² − x² = 1 crosses the ct′ axis (x = βct), ct = γ and x = βγ, so the distance from the origin on S's diagram is γ√(1 + β²) = √((1 + β²)/(1 − β²)) > 1. By symmetry, x² − (ct)² = 1 crosses the x′ axis at the same distance. Both primed units are longer than the unprimed units by the same factor.
rationales: The guide states that the scales are not the same and are defined by lines of constant space–time interval. The curve (ct)² − x² = 1 unit² crosses ct′ at ct′ = 1; on S's diagram that point lies further from the origin than ct = 1.
A student who assumes axes with the same unit share one scale picks this. Same unit does not mean same drawn scale; the scales are fixed by lines of constant interval.

A student who builds the headline results into the drawing picks this. As drawn on S's diagram, a unit on a primed axis is longer, and it is found from a line of constant interval, not by dividing by γ.

A student who maps 'time dilation' onto a stretched time axis and 'length contraction' onto a shrunk space axis picks this. Both primed units are set by the invariant hyperbolae, and on S's diagram both appear longer than the unprimed units by the same factor, √((1 + v²/c²)/(1 − v²/c²)); neither axis is shrunk.

mcqs.q: A space–time diagram for frame S has axes x and ct in light-years (ly). Frame S′ moves at 0.50c along +x; its ct′ axis and x′ axis are each tilted by the same angle towards the 45° line, the x′ axis rising 0.50 ly of ct for each 1 ly of x. Event P is at (x = 0, ct = 2.0 ly) and event Q at (x = 4.0 ly, ct = 2.0 ly). What is the order of P and Q in S′?
options: P and Q are simultaneous, because they lie on one line parallel to the x axis of S.
P occurs before Q, because Q lies further along the x′ axis, which tilts upwards.
P occurs before Q, because light from Q takes longer to reach an observer standing at x = 0.
Q occurs before P, as Q lies below the line through P parallel to the x′ axis.
mcqs.specStatementText: space–time diagrams
mcqs.explain: Lines parallel to the x′ axis join events simultaneous in S′. The line through P rises 0.50 ly per ly, so at x = 4.0 ly it is at ct = 4.0 ly. Q, at ct = 2.0 ly, lies below it, so Q is earlier in S′. Check: cΔt′ = γ(cΔt − (v/c)Δx) = 1.15 × (0 − 2.0 ly) < 0.
mcqs.working: x′-axis slope: Δ(ct)/Δx = v/c = 0.50. Line through P parallel to x′: ct = 2.0 + 0.50x → at x = 4.0 ly, ct = 4.0 ly. Q (ct = 2.0 ly) lies below → earlier in S′. Lorentz: γ = 1.155; cΔt′ = γ(0 − 0.50 × 4.0 ly) = −2.3 ly.
rationales: A student who assumes simultaneity is the same in every frame picks this. A line parallel to the x axis joins events simultaneous in S only; simultaneity in S′ is read along lines parallel to the x′ axis.
A student who reads the tilt the wrong way picks this. The upward tilt means the S′ simultaneity line through P passes above Q, so Q happens first in S′, consistent with t′ = γ(t − vx/c²).
A student who dates events by when light arrives picks this. The order of events in a frame is set by its time coordinates, not by signal arrival; in S′, Q has the earlier time coordinate.

Lines parallel to the x′ axis join events simultaneous in S′. The line through P rises 0.50 ly per ly, so at x = 4.0 ly it is at ct = 4.0 ly. Q, at ct = 2.0 ly, lies below it, so Q is earlier in S′. Check: cΔt′ = γ(cΔt − (v/c)Δx) = 1.15 × (0 − 2.0 ly) < 0.

mcqs.q: On a space–time diagram with axes x and ct, the world line of a particle moving at constant velocity makes an angle of 25° with the ct axis. What is the speed of the particle?
mcqs.specStatementText: that the angle between the world line of a moving particle and the time axis on a space–time diagram is related to the particle’s speed as given by tan θ = v/c
mcqs.explain: tan θ = v/c, with θ measured from the ct axis. v = c tan 25° = 0.466c ≈ 0.47c.
mcqs.working: v = c tan θ = c tan 25° = 0.466c ≈ 0.47c.
rationales: A student who uses sin θ gets sin 25° = 0.42. The world line moves Δx for each Δ(ct), which is opposite over adjacent: tan θ = v/c.
tan θ = v/c, with θ measured from the ct axis. v = c tan 25° = 0.466c ≈ 0.47c.
A student who measures the angle from the x axis uses tan 65° = 2.14 and gets a speed greater than c. θ is measured from the ct axis: v = c tan 25°.
A student who assumes speed is proportional to angle, with light at 45°, calculates (25/45)c = 0.56c. tan θ is not proportional to θ: v = c tan 25° = 0.47c.

mcqs.q: A student draws the world line of an electron moving at constant velocity as a straight line at 50° to the ct axis. Which evaluation is correct?
options: It cannot be correct: tan 50° ≈ 1.2, so the electron would have to move faster than light.
It cannot be correct: a line at more than 45° would mean that the electron moves back in time.
It is possible: the angle to the x axis is 40°, so its speed is c tan 40° ≈ 0.84c.
It is possible: sin 50° ≈ 0.77, so the electron is moving at a speed of about 0.77c.
mcqs.specStatementText: that the angle between the world line of a moving particle and the time axis on a space–time diagram is related to the particle’s speed as given by tan θ = v/c
mcqs.explain: tan θ = v/c gives v = 1.19c. No particle with mass can reach c, so its world line must make less than 45° with the ct axis.
mcqs.working: v/c = tan 50° = 1.19 > 1 → impossible for a massive particle. (tan 40° = 0.84; sin 50° = 0.77 are the errors.)
rationales: tan θ = v/c gives v = 1.19c. No particle with mass can reach c, so its world line must make less than 45° with the ct axis.
A student who links faster-than-light motion with time travel picks this. The line at 50° still rises in ct, so it does not go back in time; it is impossible because it means v > c.
A student who measures the angle from the x axis picks this. θ in tan θ = v/c is measured from the ct axis; at 50°, v = 1.19c, which is impossible.
A student who uses sin θ picks this. The relation is tan θ = v/c, and tan 50° = 1.19 > 1 gives a speed above c.

mcqs.q: Muons are produced 4.5 km above the ground (measured in the Earth's frame) and travel straight down at 0.995c. What is the thickness of this 4.5 km layer of atmosphere in the muons' rest frame?
mcqs.specStatementText: that muon decay experiments provide experimental evidence for time dilation and length contraction.
mcqs.explain: In the muons' frame the atmosphere moves at 0.995c, so it is contracted. γ = 1/√(1 − 0.995²) = 10.0. L = L₀/γ = 4500 m/10.0 = 450 m.
mcqs.working: γ = 1/√(1 − 0.995²) = 1/√0.009975 = 10.0. Proper length (Earth frame) L₀ = 4500 m. Muon frame: L = L₀/γ = 4500 m/10.0 = 449 m ≈ 4.5 × 10² m.
rationales: A student who multiplies by γ gets 4500 × 10.0 = 45 km. A moving length is contracted: L = L₀/γ.
A student who thinks only the muon, as the 'moving' object, is affected gives the Earth-frame value. In the muons' frame the atmosphere is moving, so it is contracted.
A student who omits the square root uses γ = 1/(1 − 0.995²) = 100 and gets 45 m. γ = 1/√0.009975 = 10.0.
In the muons' frame the atmosphere moves at 0.995c, so it is contracted. γ = 1/√(1 − 0.995²) = 10.0. L = L₀/γ = 4500 m/10.0 = 450 m.

mcqs.q: In a simplified muon experiment, muons moving at 0.995c (γ = 10.0) are counted at 1000 per hour by a detector on a mountain. An identical detector 2.25 km lower counts about 700 per hour. The muon half-life at rest is 1.5 μs, and the descent takes 7.5 μs in the Earth's frame. Which conclusion do the data support?
options: Time dilation: in the muons' own frame their half-life is dilated to 15 μs, so most survive.
Length contraction: Earth observers measure the 2.25 km drop contracted to about 225 m.
Time dilation: in the Earth frame the half-life is about 15 μs, so about 700 per hour should arrive.
Neither effect: the 1.5 μs rest half-life must be wrong, as half-life is the same in all frames.
mcqs.specStatementText: that muon decay experiments provide experimental evidence for time dilation and length contraction.
mcqs.explain: Earth frame: half-life = γ × 1.5 μs = 15 μs, so the 7.5 μs descent is 0.5 half-lives and 1000 × 2^(−0.5) ≈ 710 per hour survive, as observed. Without time dilation the descent is 5 half-lives and only about 31 per hour would arrive.
mcqs.working: Earth frame: descent time = 2250 m/(0.995 × 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) = 7.5 μs. Dilated half-life = 10.0 × 1.5 μs = 15 μs → 0.50 half-lives → 1000 × 2^(−0.50) = 7.1 × 10² per hour ≈ observed 700. No dilation: 7.5/1.5 = 5.0 half-lives → 1000 × 2^(−5.0) ≈ 31 per hour. Muon frame: drop contracted to 2250/10.0 = 225 m, crossed in 0.75 μs = 0.50 half-lives → same prediction.
rationales: A student who thinks a moving particle's time slows in its own frame picks this. In its own frame a muon is at rest with a half-life of 1.5 μs; it survives there because the atmosphere is contracted.

A student who assigns length contraction to the wrong frame picks this. The mountain is at rest in the Earth frame, so Earth observers measure 2.25 km; the contraction to 225 m is measured in the muons' frame.

Earth frame: half-life = γ × 1.5 μs = 15 μs, so the 7.5 μs descent is 0.5 half-lives and 1000 × 2^(−0.5) ≈ 710 per hour survive, as observed. Without time dilation the descent is 5 half-lives and only about 31 per hour would arrive.

A student who assumes time intervals are the same in every frame concludes the rest-frame value must be wrong. The measured half-life at rest is reliable; the data match the relativistic prediction of a dilated half-life.

mcqs.q: A cube has edges of proper length 2.0 m. It moves at 0.80c relative to an observer, parallel to one of its edges. Which statement gives the dimensions of the cube as measured by this observer?
options: Its edge along the motion is 3.3 m; its other two edges are still 2.0 m each.
Its edge along the motion is 1.2 m; its other two edges are 2.0 m each.
All three of its edges are 1.2 m, because every dimension contracts by γ.
All three of its edges are 2.0 m, because a moving object merely looks shorter.
mcqs.specStatementText: length contraction as given by L = L₀/γ
mcqs.explain: γ = 1/√(1 − 0.80²) = 1.67, so the edge parallel to the motion is measured as L = L₀/γ = 2.0/1.67 = 1.2 m. Length contraction acts only along the direction of relative motion; the two perpendicular edges keep their proper length of 2.0 m.
mcqs.working:
γ = 1/√(1 − 0.80²) = 1/√0.36 = 1/0.60 = 1.67.
Only the edge parallel to the relative velocity is contracted: L = L₀/γ = 2.0 m × 0.60 = 1.2 m.
The two edges perpendicular to the motion are unchanged at 2.0 m. The observer measures a block 1.2 m × 2.0 m × 2.0 m.
rationales: A student who multiplies by γ, as in time dilation, gets 2.0 × 1.67 = 3.3 m. Lengths are divided by γ: the moving edge is measured as L = L₀/γ = 1.2 m, shorter than its proper length.

γ = 1/√(1 − 0.80²) = 1.67, so the edge parallel to the motion is measured as L = L₀/γ = 2.0/1.67 = 1.2 m. Length contraction acts only along the direction of relative motion; the two perpendicular edges keep their proper length of 2.0 m.

A student who applies the contraction to every dimension picks this. Only the length parallel to the relative velocity is contracted; lengths perpendicular to the motion are the same in every inertial frame, so the other two edges are measured as 2.0 m.

A student who treats length contraction as an appearance caused by light travel time picks this. The contracted length is what the observer measures with rulers at rest in their own frame, after any signal delay is allowed for: the edge along the motion is genuinely measured as 1.2 m.
